unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Biological fundamentals of cancer as a genetic/evolutionary disease and general causes including endogenous stress, bad luck, and genetics.
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Everyday environmental exposures, the public debate surrounding bad luck versus environmental causes, and geographical epidemiology.
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 4 moves away from the biological definitions of cancer and endogenous mutations to focus on real-world environmental hazards, public misconceptions, and epidemiological studies.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopics 2 to 6 work together as an overarching introductory overview of cancer etiology and risk before detailed molecular mechanisms are addressed.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Carcinogenesis driven by infectious agents, pathogens, and the specific mechanism of Burkitt lymphoma.
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Dietary carcinogens and the formation of reactive DNA adducts by aflatoxin.
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 9 shifts the mechanistic focus from infectious pathogens and immune deregulation to chemical toxins found in food.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 9 is simply the next category in a continuous sequence of specific environmental carcinogens that began in subtopic 7.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Aflatoxin metabolism in the liver and bulky DNA adduct formation.
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: UV radiation damage and thymine dimer formation.
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 10 focuses on physical radiation and nucleotide excision repair rather than ingested dietary chemicals.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 10 is a single, brief subtopic providing another example within the broader survey of DNA-damaging environmental agents.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Thymine dimer formation caused by UV radiation.
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Chemical mutagens in tobacco smoke and cooked meat, xenobiotic metabolism, and tissue-specific carcinogens.
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 11 starts a detailed multi-part explanation of xenobiotic metabolism via the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and CYP enzymes.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Tobacco and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are standard examples continuing the overarching walkthrough of environmental mutagens.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Chemical mutagens requiring xenobiotic activation to cause DNA transversions and tissue-specific damage.
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Non-mutagenic carcinogens, chronic inflammation, and the distinction between initiators and promoters.
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 14 introduces a major conceptual transition from direct mutagens (initiators) to non-mutagenic inflammatory agents (promoters).
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: The initiator-promoter paradigm directly builds upon the preceding mechanisms to explain how microenvironmental factors drive tumorigenesis alongside mutagens.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Experimental evidence for the initiator-promoter hypothesis and protein kinase C activation.
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Host developmental stages and life-stage tissue susceptibility to carcinogens, followed by a summary of mutational mechanisms.
unsureMarks.caseForStart: Subtopic 16 shifts attention to host biology, developmental windows, and life-stage susceptibility.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Host developmental factors and the concluding summary in subtopic 17 synthesize the entire mechanistic segment on how mutagens and promoters operate.

topics.label: Lecture Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: The subtopic sets up the lecture series, introduces the speaker, and outlines the core learning outcomes regarding environmental carcinogenesis.

topics.label: Cancer Etiology, Bad Luck, and Epidemiological Evidence
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics provide an overarching framework of cancer causation, balancing endogenous genetic mutations, bad luck, and epidemiological evidence of environmental risks across populations.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Carcinogenesis: Mutagens, Initiators, and Promoters
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail the biological and biochemical mechanisms by which specific environmental agents—pathogens, dietary toxins, radiation, chemical mutagens, and inflammatory promoters—cause and promote cancer.

topics.label: Methodologies for Assessing Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics evaluate the scientific methods used to prove and detect carcinogenicity, including mutational signatures, biobank epidemiology, animal toxicity studies, and the Ames test.

topics.label: Summary and Risk-Benefit Conclusion
topics.groupedBecause: The subtopic delivers final summary remarks framing carcinogenic risk versus everyday benefits and closes the lecture.
